sections.heading: ABSTRACT:
sections.text: To acquire the synergy effects between Sn and Cu for the jointly high Faradaic efficiency and current density, we develop a novel strategy to design the Sn-Cu alloy catalyst via a decorated co-electrodeposition method for CO2 electroreduction to formate. The Sn-Cu alloy shows high formate Faradaic efficiency of 82.3%±2.1% and total C1 products Faradaic efficiency of 90.0%±2.7% at −1.14 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). The current density and mass activity of formate reach as high as (79.0±0.4) mA cm−2 and (1490.6±7.5) mA mg−1 at −1.14 V vs. RHE. Theoretical calculations suggest that Sn-Cu alloy can obtain high Faradaic efficiency for CO2 electroreduction by suppressing the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction and that the formate formation follows the path of CO2 → HCOO* → HCOOH. The stepped (211) surface of Sn-Cu alloy is beneficial towards selective formate production. Keywords: Electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction reaction; Synergy effects; Sn-Cu alloy; Mass activity; Formate

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) provides an attractive approach for renewable energy storage and CO2 conversion to valuable chemicals [1−4]. Currently, C1 chemicals (e.g., formate and CO) production is identified as the most practicable and potentially profitable pathway of CO2RR [5−17]. In particular, formate is usually used as a kinetically stable liquid fuel in
3 fuel cells, because of the high hydrogen content and easy handling (e.g., transport and storage) at room temperature [8]. Furthermore, formate is also identified as a key intermediate and important starting material for the chemical synthesis industry [18]. As a consequence, CO2RR to formate is of extraordinary significance. At present, various metals such as Sn, Cu, In, Bi, Co and Pd etc., have been investigated as catalysts for CO2RR to formate [1,5−12,19−29]. Nonetheless, the Faradaic efficiency and mass activity of these catalysts are generally limited even in a high overpotential window [19−30]. So far, Sn catalysts have exhibited desirable Faradaic efficiency for catalyzing formate production [5−8,31,32]. In the meantime, Cu catalysts not only selectively yield C2+ (e.g. alcohol and n-propanol) products, but also efficiently catalyze CO2RR to formate with an appreciable Faradaic efficiency [3,4,20]. Although these catalysts own appreciable Faradaic efficiencies towards formate at high overpotentials, they still suffer from poor mass activity. Alloying Sn or Cu with the other element is a potential avenue to promote the CO2RR performance, which is attained by modulating the binding energies of reaction intermediates through tailoring surface electronic structure of the alloys [33−35]. For instance, Pd-Sn alloy catalysts inhibited the competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), whereas selectively improved the CO2RR performance [36]. Au-Sn alloys achieved a high formate Faradaic efficiency [37], and Ag-Sn alloys enhanced the Faradaic efficiency and current density
4 for producing formate compared with exclusive Ag or Sn catalyst [38]. However, these alloys still suffer from low mass activity, which is probably caused by the electrode preparation techniques. Generally, most CO2RR electrodes utilizing electrodeposition method are prepared by adding extraneous metal cation in the electrolyte solution mixed with the surfactants and buffering agents of organic compounds for long-time electrodeposition (e.g., 20 h) [5,8,12], which is likely to incur the inferior adhesion between the conductive substrates and catalysts. The conventional electrodeposition process will also result in a low utilization of catalysts and degrading their electrocatalytic activities [39], because partial catalysts are inaccessible to the CO2 reactant and inactive for CO2RR. Herein, we put forward a useful route to promote the CO2RR mass activity by a modified electrodeposition of Sn-Cu alloy, in which the Cu sources come from the self-dissolution of Cu substrate itself. The Sn-Cu alloy catalyst demonstrates the highest formate mass activity of (1490.6±7.5) mA mg−1 among the reported non-noble metal catalysts [5,6,19−22,30−32], with high Faradaic efficiency and stability at −1.14 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). Density functional theory (DFT) calculations indicate that Sn-Cu alloy can obtain high Faradaic efficiency and current density for CO2RR by suppressing the HER and that the formate formation on Sn-Cu alloy follows the path of CO2 → HCOO* → HCOOH. The stepped (211) surface of Sn-Cu
5 alloy, with low hydrogen evolution rate, is eventually selective towards formate production. 2. Experimental

sections.heading: 2.1. Reagents
sections.text: Stannous mono-sulphate (SnSO4), sulfuric acid (H2SO4), hydrochloric acid (HCl), potassium chloride (KCl), potassium sulphate (K2SO4), acetone (CH3COCH3) and ethanol (C2H5OH) were obtained from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Cu foam with a thickness of 1.0 mm was obtained from Jiayisheng Electronics Co., Ltd. Electrolytic tin sheets were provided by Maggi metallic material Co., Ltd. Carbon fiber cloth (CFC) was provided by Shanghai Hesen electric Co., Ltd. All chemicals were analytical grade and used without further purification.

sections.heading: 2.2. Electrode fabrication
sections.text:
The Sn-Cu alloy/Cu foam and Sn/Cu foam electrodes were synthesized using a facile electrodeposition of Sn-Cu alloy and Sn on Cu foam substrates. The electrodeposition experiments were measured in the electrochemical 3-electrode cell by computerized potentiostat (Autolab PGSTAT 302N). An electrolytic tin sheet (15 cm2) was served as counter electrode (CE). A saturated Ag/AgCl electrode was used as reference electrode (RE). The Cu foam (1 cm2) was employed as working electrode (WE). The aqueous solution for electrodeposition contained 0.2 mol L–1 SnSO4 and 1.5 mol L–1 H2SO4. A constant current of –4.0 A cm–2 was applied to the working electrode for 0.01 –
6 60 s. The Cu foam was ultrasonically cleaned with acetone, 6.0 mol L–1 HCl, ethanol and then rinsed in deionized water successively, named as preliminary treatment. Before electrodeposition, all the pretreated Cu foam substrates were immersed in the acidic solution of 0.2 mol L–1 SnSO4 and 1.5 mol L–1 H2SO4 for 2 min to acquire its own Cu2+ ions source. During the immersion process, the contact of cuprous oxide formed by spontaneous oxide of Cu substrate surface in air with sulfuric acid in the electrolyte leads to its disproportionated reaction as follows [40]: Cu2O + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O + Cu For comparison, Sn/CFC electrode was fabricated on the CFC substrate via the same electrodeposition process. The electrodeposition conditions were the same as those on Cu foam substrate. The Sn loadings on CFC were controlled by the electrodeposition time. Prior to electrodeposition, the CFC was also ultrasonically cleaned with acetone, 6.0 mol L–1 HCl, ethanol and then rinsed in deionized water successively.

sections.heading: 2.3. Physicochemical characterization
sections.text:
The structure of as-prepared catalysts was characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD, PANalytical X’pert PPR) with Cu Kα radiation source (λ=1.5418 Å). The morphologies of deposited catalysts were examined using field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, JSM-7800F) equipped with an energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM), High-resolution TEM (HRTEM), bright field and annular
7 dark field scanning TEM (BF and ADF-STEM), and energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) elemental maps were recorded by JEOL JEM-2100 microscope with an accelerating voltage of 200 kV (for TEM and HRTEM images) and JEOL JEM-F200 field emission microscope (for BF-STEM, ADF-STEM and EDX elemental maps). All the catalyst loadings were detected using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES, PerkinElmer). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) tests were acquired by the Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250Xi spectrometer. The binding energy of enthetic carbon was calibrated through the C 1s character at 284.6 eV and analyzed by XPSPEAK41 software. The X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectra at Sn K (E0 = 27,940 eV) edge was collected at BL14W1 beamline of Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF) operated at 3.5 GeV under “top-up” mode with a constant current of 260 mA. The absorption edge of pure Sn foil was used as a reference to calibrate the energy. The Sn-K edge XANES spectra of the catalysts were collected under ambient conditions in a fluorescence mode. For the XANES part, background subtraction and normalization procedures were carried out to process the experimental absorption coefficients as function of energies μ(E), which is described as “normalized absorption” with E0 for the measured samples. 2.4. CO2RR performance measurements CO2RR performance measurements were carried out utilizing the 3-electrode gastight system in an H-cell filled with 0.5 mol L–1 KCl solution at
8 the cathodic compartment and 0.25 mol L–1 K2SO4 solution at the anodic compartment, separating by Nafion 115 membrane. The use of 0.25 mol L–1 K2SO4 solution instead of 0.5 mol L–1 KCl solution as the anolyte can avoid the generation of chlorine gas. The as-obtained Sn-Cu alloy/Cu foam or Sn/Cu foam electrodes (1 cm2) acted as WE. The platinum wire and Ag/AgCl (3.0 mol L–1 KCl) were used as CE and RE, respectively. All the potentials were controlled by computerized potentiostat (Autolab PGSTAT 302N) and tested versus Ag/AgCl RE. The reference potentials were converted to RHE with iR compensation using E(RHE) = E(Ag/AgCl) + 0.210 + 0.0591 × pH. The catholyte was 0.5 mol L–1 KCl solution purged with 5% N2/CO2 at 20 mL min–1 flow rate and final pH value was 4.0. The anolyte was 0.25 mol L–1 K2SO4 solution purged with pure CO2 at 20 mL min–1 and the final pH value was adjusted to 4.0 by adding 0.035 mmol L–1 H2SO4. Each applied constant potential electrolysis was persistent for 30 min after delivering CO2 into the electrolyte in both compartments for 30 min. Both catholyte and anolyte volume was 40 mL and magnetic stirrer was stirred with the rotation rate of ~2000 r min–1 in cathodic part during CO2RR measurements. To obtain the electrochemical surface area (ECSA) [5,6], the roughness factor (Rf) of the as-prepared electrodes can be acquired according to the equation: ECSA = Rf × S [1,41], where S was usually corresponding to their geometric area (S=1 cm2, in this work). According to the double-layer capacitance (Cdl) of a smooth oxide surface per square centimeter (60 μF cm–
9 2) [41,42], Rf was calculated using the equation Rf = Cdl/60 μF. The Cdl was determined via plotting the ∆j (ja–jc) against the scan rate of cyclic voltammagrams, where ja is the double-layer anodic current, jc is the double-layer cathodic current from cyclic voltammetry in a narrow potential window. The gas products of CO2RR were measured via an on-line micro gas chromatograph (GC, Agilent 490). Ar was served as the carrier gas and N2 was employed as the internal standard gas. The CO and H2 partial current densities were obtained by GC peaks as followed [2]: ,𝑗CO = peak area 𝛼 × flow rate × 2𝐹𝑝0 𝑅𝑇 × (electrode area) –1 ,𝑗H2 = peak area 𝛽 × flow rate × 2𝐹𝑝0 𝑅𝑇 × (electrode area) –1 where α and β are conversion factors for CO and H2, R is the molar gas constant (8.314 J mol–1 K–1), p0 = 1.013 bar and T = 298 K. Formate was measured by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, Bruker AVANCE III 400 MHz) spectrometer. 1H spectrum was tested with water suppression by a pre-saturation method, while formate was quantified on the linear relationship between its concentration and relative area vs. 3-(trimethylsilyl)-1-propanesulfonic acid sodium salt. Faradaic efficiency (fFormate) of the formate was calculated as below: fFormate = QFormate/Qtotal = zF×nFormate/(I× t), where QFormate is the amount of consumed charge to produce formate, Qtotal is the total amount of consumed charge, z is the electron
10
transfer number needed to produce formate (z = 2), F is the Faraday constant, nFormate is total amount of the formed formate, I is current and t is working time. 2.5. Computational methods
Electronic structure calculations based on DFT were carried out using the
Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) [43], with the projector-augmented wave (PAW) scheme [44] and generalized gradient approximation (GGA) [45] at the level of revised PBE functional [46]. All calculations in this work were carried out with a plane-wave basis with cutoff of 450 eV and the k-point grids of (12×12×12) and (4×4×1), sampled with the Monkhorst-Pack scheme for bulk and surface optimization [47], respectively. The lattice constants for face-centered cubic (FCC) Cu and Sn were determined to be 3.62 and 4.85 Å, respectively. The (211) and (111) surfaces are built using periodically repeated unit cells p(4×3) and p(3×3), respectively, with the thickness of three layers. The bottom two layers are fixed, while the adsorbates and the top two layers are allowed to relax until the maximum residual force is less than 0.05 eV Å–1 in any directions. A 15 Å vacuum region was used to guarantee the slab separation.
Based on this setup, the electronic structure of bimetallic Cu-Sn and the
Sn substitution on a Cu surface (namely SnCu) were calculated. In the meanwhile, we introduced other transition metals for comparison, such as Ag, Pt, Ni, Pd and Rh, to establish a general feature. The DFT parameters used for these metals are the same with that for pure Cu.
11
The adsorption energy (*Eb) was defined as
*Eb = *Etotal – *Eslab – (x*Eslab + y*EO + z*EH ),
where the *Eslab and *Etotal mean the total energies of the surfaces with adsorbates and clean surfaces, respectively. The elemental energies for carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen were referred to gas phases CO, H2O and H2. The number of carbon, oxygen and hydrogen atoms in the adsorbates is represented by x, y and z.
The free energy change for each elementary step is given by
ΔG = ΔE + ΔEZPE – TΔS,
where T is the absolute temperature, ΔE is the electronic energies, ΔEZPE is the zero-point energy correction, and ΔS is the entropy change. A room temperature of 298 K was used in this work.
In order to analyze the energetics of elementary steps with a
proton-coupled electron transfer, the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) was used [48]. We relate the chemical potential for the reaction (H+ + e–) to that of ½ H2 (½ H2 ⇌ H+ + e–) by using standard hydrogen electrode as the reference state. 3. Results and discussion
Sn-Cu alloy catalyst was synthesized through a decorated
co-electrodeposition of Sn2+ and Cu2+ ions on Cu foam in 0.2 mol L–1 SnSO4 and 1.5 mol L–1 H2SO4 solution (Scheme 1). The key point of catalyst preparation is the utilization of disproportionated reaction of cuprous oxide that
12
formed by spontaneous oxide of Cu substrate surface in air. XRD analysis indicates that the Sn-Cu alloy (JCPDS No. 45-1488) is successfully prepared on Cu foam via electrodeposition for 0.01 s (Fig. S1 online). The metallic Cu substrate and its surface cuprous oxide can also be monitored from the XRD pattern. SEM images display the Sn-Cu alloy nanoparticles finely disperse on the surface of Cu foam (Fig. 1a and Fig. S2 online). Analysis of STEM images illustrates the presence of alloy particles with average size of 4 nm (Fig. 1b and 1c), and the corresponding EDX elemental maps further confirm it (Fig. 1d–f and Fig. S3 online). HRTEM image shows numerous lattice fringes with the d spacing of 0.30 nm measured by two neighboring crystal lattice planes, corresponding to the (22Ī) interplanar spacing of Cu6Sn5 alloy phase, indicative of the formation of Sn-Cu alloy (Fig. S4 online).
To compare the CO2RR performance of Sn-Cu alloy and Sn catalysts on
the identical substrate of Cu foam, we prepared pure Sn catalysts via extending the electrodeposition time of Sn2+ ions to acquire Sn species completely coated on Cu foam surface. Hence, the Sn-containing catalysts with various electrodeposition time were examined accordingly on Cu foam substrate and their loadings (Table S1 online) were analyzed by ICP-OES. XRD analysis confirms that the Cu foam substrate after pretreatment contains cuprous oxide on its surface, which can offer Cu2+ sources disproportionated by acidic electrolyte for the closely following co-electrodeposition of Sn2+ and Cu2+ for 0.01 s (Fig. S5 online). Additional EDX elemental maps analysis and
13
SEM results show that pure Sn catalysts are entirely coated on the surface of Cu foam after electrodeposition for 1 s and continue to develop like seedlings ultimately grown into tree-like morphology, which can be easily controlled by the electrodeposition parameters (e.g., deposition time) (Figs. S6 and S7 online).
CO2RR performance of Sn-Cu alloy and Sn catalysts including their Cu
foam substrates were measured in an H-cell (Fig. S8 online). The products Faradaic efficiencies at pretreated Cu foam substrate are obtained in the potential ranges from −0.75 to −1.14 V vs. RHE and shown in Fig. 2a. The detected products of CO2RR are formate, CO and H2, which are quantified by NMR spectroscopy and on-line GC, respectively. The onset potential of CO2RR to formate is −0.85 V vs. RHE. Over the Cu foam substrate, the formate Faradaic efficiency is kept below 30.0%, whereas Faradaic efficiency of the competitive HER maintains higher than 30.0% in the whole tested potential window. The geometrical partial current density of all the products are calculated lower than 5.3 mA cm−2 (Fig. 2b), suggesting that the CO2RR performance of Cu foam substrate is rather poor. In other words, the pure Cu catalyst including its surface cuprous oxide can’t provide an effective performance for CO2RR to formate. In contrast, Sn-Cu alloy catalyst yields formate as the major product with a Faradaic efficiency of 82.3%±2.1% and competitive HER is significantly suppressed at −1.14 V vs. RHE. The total C1 Faradaic efficiencies attain 90.0%±2.7% at −1.14 V vs. RHE (Fig. 2c). In order
14
to demonstrate CO2RR performance of the only deposited Sn-Cu alloy catalyst, the background current density of Cu foam substrate (Fig. 2b) is eliminated. The geometrical partial current density and mass activity after deducting the Cu foam background of formate, CO and H2 on the Sn-Cu alloy catalyst are shown in Fig. S9 (online) and Fig. 2d. The formate geometrical current density and mass activity of Sn-Cu alloy catalyst achieve (79.0±0.4) mA cm−2 (Fig. S9 online) and (1490.6±7.5) mA mg−1 (Fig. 2d) at −1.14 V vs. RHE, respectively. To investigate the inherent relationship between the Sn-Cu alloy and Sn catalysts on Cu foam, we explore the CO2RR performance of pure Sn catalysts through prolonging the electrodeposition time of Sn to completely coat Cu foam substrate surface (Figs. S5−S7 online). All the catalysts with various electrodeposition time demonstrate a high Faradaic efficiency of formate with more than 82.3% and Faradaic efficiency of C1 products attains more than 90.0% at –1.14 V vs. RHE (Fig. 2e). The geometrical partial current density of formate is slightly increased in spite of increasing the electrodeposition time by 6000 times longer from 0.01 to 60 s (Fig. S10 online). Interestingly, the formate mass activity is promptly improved through decreasing the electrodeposition time less than 1 s to make the Sn-Cu alloy species expose their surface and efficiently catalyze the CO2RR (Fig. 2f), which is in good agreement with their EDX elemental maps result (Fig. S7 online). Therefore, compared with the pure Sn catalysts on Cu foam, the Sn-Cu alloy catalyst displays a much higher formate mass activity.
15
In addition, to further understand the catalytic role of Sn-Cu alloy, we also
prepare pure Sn catalyst on the nonmetallic CFC substrate (Figs. S11−S13 online) with catalyst loading (Table S2 online) similar to that on Cu foam (Table S1 online). Compared with Sn on CFC, Sn-Cu alloy catalyst shows a higher formate Faradaic efficiency and suppresses hydrogen production (Fig. 3a). Notably, formate mass activity of the Sn-Cu alloy ((1490.6±7.5) mA mg−1) is much higher than that of Sn on CFC ((385.7±11.7) mA mg−1) at –1.14 V vs. RHE (Fig. 3b). Besides, the electrochemical surface area (ECSA) [1,5,6] is also examined for evaluating the intrinsic activity of Sn and Sn-Cu alloy (Fig. S14 online and Fig. 3c). The geometrical partial current density of formate is corrected by their ECSA for comparison (Fig. 3d). Markedly, the Sn-Cu alloy not only demonstrates higher ECSA than Sn, but also exhibits three times higher intrinsic activity that may be due to the inherent catalytic role of Sn-Cu alloy. During 660 min electrocatalysis test, the Sn-Cu alloy achieves a relatively stable total geometrical current density of ~ 100 mA cm−2 at –1.14 V vs. RHE (Fig. S15 online). In contrast to CO2RR performance of the Sn-based catalysts reported so far [5,6,19,30−32,35−38], the Sn-Cu alloy in this work exhibits an excellent activity, indicating the Sn-Cu alloy is promising for the prospective applications of CO2RR. In-situ XANES spectra results suggest that the Sn element keeps its positive charge state under the CO2RR condition (Fig. S16 online), in agreement with ex-situ XPS result (Fig. S17 online).
16
To understand the chemical origins of enhanced formate selectivity, we
have performed DFT calculations to analyze the reaction mechanism and pathways. Although several transition metal electrodes (including Cu and Sn) have been reported previously, the reaction mechanism of formate selectivity is still obscure. Herein, we first established a correlation [49] between *ECOOH and reaction free energies (see Figs. S18 and S19 online) to explore the general trends of various elementary steps over different elemental metals, and then justify the ΔG-limiting step for a specific catalyst. As our theoretical models and method has been validated, we further addressed the electronic structures and reactivity over CuSn alloy. Finally, the activity and selectivity trend of formic acid over the CuSn alloy have been analyzed, for both (211) step and (111) terrace surfaces.
It is well known that formic acid can be formed by two different paths,
namely CO2 → HCOO* → HCOOH and CO2 → COOH* → HCOOH [50,51]. As shown in Fig. 4a, the solid red lines represent the ΔG-limiting step in formic acid formation, where the metals with lower ΔG-limiting step indicate a more favorable formation of formic acid. We can see that the formic acid synthesis is most likely to obey the COOH* path on the (211) facet of catalysts with strong *ECOOH (shadowed), while the HCOO* path becomes more preferable in the region with weaker *ECOOH (blank). The same trend also appears in the (111) surface, as shown in Fig. 4b, indicating that the formation of formic acid can follow two different paths on both step and terrace surfaces.
17
As shown in Fig. 4a, the formation of formic acid follows the reaction
mechanism via *COOH path on the Cu(211) surface, while the COOH* intermediate can also be selectively dissociated to form *CO as a competitive step. The reaction free energies of *COOH formation is higher than the *COOH dissociation on the Cu(211) surface, indicating that the *COOH formation is the ΔG-limiting step and CO formation is much easier to occur. However, the CO adsorption energy and coverage on Cu is appropriate, avoiding the surface from CO poisoning, which enhances its ability to be further reduced to alcohols and hydrocarbons, in good agreement with experimental results [53,54]. As for the Cu(111) surface, the formic acid formation is via the HCOO* intermediate.
For Sn(211) surface, the formic acid formation follows another reaction
mechanism via HCOO* path, in accordance with the results reported by Feaster et al. [50] where it shows that Sn is the best catalyst for selectively producing formate, compared to other elemental metals, such as Cu, Pt and Ni, consistent with our findings too. As shown in Fig. 4a, the HCOO* hydrogenation can be regarded as the ΔG-limiting step, which indicates that the COOH* formation is less favorable, and the CO production by COOH* dissociation will be inhibited. In addition, the competing hydrogen evolution is also not dominant due to the low coverage of adsorbed H* on the surface, where the H adsorption energy on Sn is quite weak (+0.60 eV).
18
All the analysis above shows a weaker COOH* binding, compared to Sn
electrode, is beneficial by promoting the HCOO* and suppressing CO* evolution to higher HCOOH selectivity. For the CuSn alloys, we modeled the synergistic effect of the Sn substitution on a perfect (111) and (211) Cu surface. We considered three substitutional sites on (211) surface, from the top site of the step to the bottom site of the step. Herein, the stability of the alloying surface was determined by the relative substitution. The result in Fig. S20a online shows that the replacement of the Cu atom at the top of the (211) surface by a Sn atom is the most stable one, compared to the substitution of the middle and bottom atoms, while for (111) surface shown in Fig. S20b (online), the substitutional Sn atom at subsurface results in significantly less stable structures. In other words, the low coordinated Cu atoms at edges and corners are more easily replaced than those in subsurface or bulk. Therefore, the SnCu(211) surface was modeled by replacing Cu atoms at the edge of (211) surface (labeled as 1SnCu211 and 3SnCu shown in Fig. 5a). Moreover, the SnCu(111) surface was shown in Fig. 5b, labeled as 1SnCu111 and 9SnCu.
As shown in Fig. 4c, the *ECOOH on the 1SnCu211 surface is between pure
Cu and pure Sn. It was obvious *ECOOH on the SnCu(211) surface becomes significantly weaker due to the ligand effect. Thus, the Sn electrode with Cu alloying results in stronger adsorption affinity of COOH compared to pure Sn. In this case, the formation of formic acid becomes less favorable on 1SnCu211 surface since the reaction free energy of the HCOO* hydrogenation increases.
19
However, for the 3SnCu catalyst, the *ECOOH becomes weaker, more close to the lowest reaction energy. This indicates the 3SnCu surface has a higher formate activity, and the optimized structure of adsorbates on 3SnCu surface is shown in Fig. S21 (online). At the same time, the reaction energy of forming H2 on this surface is higher than that of forming formic acid, which indicates a high selectivity of forming formic acid, rationalizing well experimental observations.
Fig. 4d shows that the *ECOOH on both Cu(111) and Sn(111) surfaces is
very similar. The formation of formic acid on the terrace of Cu and Sn electrodes follows the HCOO* path. The experimental results show that after doping Sn on Cu surface, the selectivity of formic acid increases, and the selectivity of H2 decreases correspondingly. Especially, the selectivity of formic acid reaches 82.3%±2.1%. It can be seen that 1SnCu111 is almost at the point with the lowest reaction energy, possessing the great activity. However, as the Cu doped Sn catalysts, the selectivity of the formic acid of the catalyst decreases, and the selectivity of H2 increases. This is might due to the change in the active phase of the catalyst surface. In other words, the surface of the 1SnCu111 evolves to the surface of the 9SnCu because Cu is more likely to be doped in the bulk phase of Sn rather than the surface. The Sn-Cu alloy surface is most likely covered by all Sn atoms, consistent with the structure of 9SnCu as shown in Fig. 5b. However, it should be noted that although the reaction free energy of formic acid on 1SnCu111 is low, and the H2 production is always
20
lower than that of formic acid. This indicates the (111) surface is not likely to be the active sites for high selectivity of formic acid formation.
It should be noted that the *ECOOH in 1SnCu111 surface is not between pure
Cu and pure Sn, that is, the *ECOOH is weaker in 1SnCu111 than in pure Sn. However, the *ECOOH in 1SnCu211 surface is between pure Cu and pure Sn. The lattice constant of Cu (3.62 Å) is shorter than Sn (4.85 Å). The adsorption of species is weakened since the Sn doping to Cu(111) surface exerts a compressive stress on the surface. As reported by Li et al. [55], the bonding of adsorbates on a compressed surface will be reduced, compared to that on extended surfaces. And it has large effect on the closed packed surfaces and almost no effects on the edges and steps, well explaining our calculated results on both (111) and (211) surfaces. 4. Conclusion
In summary, we have displayed a novel strategy to design the Sn-Cu alloy
catalyst through a decorated co-electrodeposition method to attain the selective CO2RR to formate with high performance. The Sn-Cu alloy plays an important role in maintaining its high Faradaic efficiency and current density towards CO2RR to formate. The Sn-Cu alloy suppresses H2 and CO evolution and promotes the formate production with Faradaic efficiency of 82.3%±2.1% at −1.14 V vs. RHE. The formate mass activity reaches (1490.6±7.5) mA mg−1 at −1.14 V vs. RHE, outperforming all the reported Sn-based catalysts. DFT calculations suggest that the formate formation on Sn-Cu alloy catalyst follows
21
the path of CO2 → HCOO* → HCOOH. The stepped (211) surface of Sn-Cu alloy is selective towards formate production. This strategy can be further introduced to exploit other alloy catalysts with controllable reaction routes.
